archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: He does his best work after the play breaks down, holding the ball and escaping for chunk scrambles. His designed runs and timing passing from the pocket lag well behind that.

report.headline: His legs keep drives alive; his pocket passing and sacks keep Miami winless.
report.take:
Willis earned the Miami job on two tiny Green Bay relief stints that were about as good as quarterback play gets: 10.19 yards per attempt in 2024 and 12.06 in 2025, with no interceptions either year. Five starts and 130 attempts later, the larger sample looks much more like his 2022 Titans tape than the Packers cameos. He is 39th of 43 in EPA per dropback (-0.201) and 39th in CPOE (-7.72). His 9.7% sack rate and 3 lost fumbles sit near the bottom of the league. Miami is 0-5.

The positive part of his game is real, and it is specific. His 17 scrambles have gained 167 yards and 8 first downs at +0.755 EPA each, and that drives his rank of third among quarterbacks in rushing yards. His designed runs average 1.9 yards with a 40% stuff rate, so the value comes from improvisation, not the run game. As a passer, the intermediate window works: +0.465 EPA and positive CPOE on throws of 10-19 air yards. Everything else is poor:
- Screens and throws behind the line return -0.385 EPA.
- Deep balls connect 17.9% of the time, 20.9 points under expectation.

The numbers that look like scheme or bad luck mostly aren't. The sacks are a career trait, not a 2026 problem. His pressure-to-sack rate was 0.435, 0.667 and 0.6 in his three prior seasons, and he holds the ball 3.17 seconds. That long clock is what produces both the scrambles and the sacks. This year the sacks are winning that trade, since 14 sacks plus 5 turnover-worthy fumbles cost more than the scrambles gain. Garbage time isn't flattering his line either. With the game within one score his EPA is -0.331, worse than his -0.13 when trailing by nine or more. Miami also passes 11.1 points less than expected (31st), which tells you how little the staff trusts the dropback game. The defense ranks 30th against the pass and keeps forcing him into catch-up mode anyway.

The last two starts were his worst as a passer, at -12.4 and -11.4 EPA. He did rush for 74 yards against Cincinnati, which says the offense is leaning harder on his legs. There is some signal for a better plan in the Week 2 game at San Francisco: his only positive passing EPA of the year came with an 8.7% aggressiveness rate and 6.4 intended air yards. Simply put, he was better when he threw short and fast. Unless the bye produces that kind of quick-game reset, expect the same shape of quarterback: useful rushing floor, volatile and below-average passing.

strengths.title: Scrambles that move the chains
strengths.body: When the pocket breaks down he is a real threat, turning 10.6% of dropbacks into scrambles worth +0.755 EPA apiece, with 8 first downs on 17 tries. He has posted 120-plus rushing yards in each prior season despite tiny samples, so the athleticism is durable. That makes this the most sustainable piece of his production.

strengths.title: Intermediate throws hold up
strengths.body: Between 10 and 19 air yards he is completing 59.3% with positive CPOE and +0.465 EPA per attempt, the one passing band where he beats expectation. On 27 attempts that is a hint rather than a fact. It fits the Green Bay version of him, though, and it is the area a bye-week game plan should build around.

concerns.title: Sacks are a career-long trait
concerns.body: He has taken 14 sacks on 161 dropbacks and converts 31.4% of pressures into sacks. That is not new: every prior season showed a pressure-to-sack rate between 0.435 and 0.667. It is the cost of holding the ball to hunt scrambles, and right now the sacks, including 6 on third down and 4 in the red zone, outweigh what the scrambles return.

concerns.title: Deep ball and accuracy are broken
concerns.body: Only 5 of 28 deep attempts have been completed, 20.9 points under expectation. His 14.6% bad-throw rate ranks 27th of 36. The Packers-era accuracy (85.7% completions in 2025) came on too few throws to trust, and 130 attempts now say he is a below-expectation thrower.

concerns.title: Ball security and close-game play
concerns.body: He has 3 lost fumbles (40th of 43) and 5 turnover-worthy fumbles alongside 4 interceptions. His passing is worst exactly when games are still competitive, at -0.331 EPA within one score. The fumble count can regress somewhat, but the handling issues tie back to the same extended-play style.

trend.note: He held around 200-220 passing yards in the first three games, then fell to 85 and 137 with his two worst passing EPA games (-12.4, -11.4). His rushing climbed to a season-high 74 yards in Week 5, so the offense is leaning harder on his legs.

nextGame.headline: Coming off a bye into the league's second-best sack defense
nextGame.body:
The Jets are the wrong opponent for a quarterback whose biggest flaw is sacks. Their 9.1% sack rate ranks 2nd in the league. They have held quarterbacks to 209 passing yards a game, the 3rd-fewest, and their run defense ranks 7th by EPA, which squeezes his already weak designed runs. The openings are underneath: they rank 22nd in EPA allowed on short passes and 29th against WR3s. That points toward a quick-game plan like the one that worked in San Francisco. Their tight-end defense ranks first, which takes away Dulcich, his most efficient target at +0.22 EPA. It's divisional and on the road; Miami had a Week 6 bye, so a 14-day rest.

Availability cuts both ways. Miami lists WR Caleb Douglas (89% snap share over his 2 games) as out with an expected return on game day, and LG Jonah Savaiinaea (85% of snaps, ankle) as questionable with the same date. Losing Savaiinaea would hurt most against this front. On the Jets side, edge rusher Braiden McGregor is on IR and Joseph Ossai (45% of snaps) is questionable with an ankle, which could thin the rush rotation a little. The Jets' offense has Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell and G Dylan Parham out but tagged for an October 18 return. If they stay out, a weaker Jets attack against Miami's 30th-ranked pass defense could keep the game closer and the play-calling more balanced.

keyMatchups.title: Jets pass rush vs. long clock
keyMatchups.body: New York gets home on 9.1% of dropbacks, while Willis takes a sack on 9.7% of his and holds the ball 3.17 seconds. Expect multiple sacks unless Miami shortens his drops. Each sack also takes away a potential scramble, his best play.

keyMatchups.title: Quick game against soft underneath
keyMatchups.body: The Jets give up +0.095 EPA on short throws (22nd), the softest part of their coverage. Willis has been roughly neutral on 0-9 yard throws, and the outlook improves if he plays that way. Whether Miami calls it after the bye is the key coaching question.

keyMatchups.title: Dulcich into the top TE defense
keyMatchups.body: His best target by EPA, Greg Dulcich, faces a defense allowing -0.31 EPA per play to tight ends, best in the league. With Douglas likely missing, more volume probably shifts to Washington (36 targets, -0.012 EPA) and lesser options.

nextGame.watch: How fast the ball comes out on early downs: under three seconds means Miami adjusted; another long-clock game against this rush means four-plus sacks.

restOfSeason.body:
The rushing floor is real. Scrambles and 6.89 yards per carry come from athleticism he has shown every season, and they should keep him around 30-45 rushing yards with occasional short touchdowns. The passing should stay below average. His CPOE and bad-throw rates fit his 2022 starts better than the Packers cameos, and the deep ball isn't coming back at 17.9%. Two things could plausibly move up: the 1.5% TD rate on more red-zone trips, and the fumbles lost, which tend to swing back toward average.

Game script works against him. Miami's defense ranks 28th overall and 30th against the pass, so he will keep dropping back while trailing. That inflates his attempts and sacks more than his efficiency. Fantasy value depends on rushing touchdowns, and his job security depends on whether the intermediate passing can carry more weight.
swingFactors: A quick-game shift that cuts the sack rate
Caleb Douglas and Jonah Savaiinaea returning

bets.reason: He takes a sack on 9.7% of dropbacks with a 31.4% pressure-to-sack rate, a trait across every season. The Jets' 9.1% sack rate ranks 2nd. Thinner Jets edge depth (McGregor on IR, Ossai questionable) is the only thing holding this below an 8.

The Jets allow the 3rd-fewest passing yards to quarterbacks (209 a game). Willis has averaged 111 over his last two games, and Miami passes 11.1 points below expectation. His top wideout by snaps, Douglas, is listed out.

He has thrown 4 interceptions on a 3.1% rate, with picks in 3 of 5 starts. A heavy pass rush forcing hurried throws adds risk. The Jets' pass defense is only mid-pack (18th by EPA), so the edge is modest.

confidence.note: Five starts and 130 attempts; the career sack trait is stable, but the passing sample is still small and there's no line yet.
